principles: A subnet scan seeks breadth or discovery; a flood primarily creates sustained load or resource pressure.
Many sources in one subnet do not by themselves establish DDoS.
High request volume does not by itself establish DDoS; legitimate bursts and retries exist.
DDoS hypotheses require correlated traffic pressure plus service-impact or resource-pressure evidence when available.
Recon can precede a flood, coexist with it, or be unrelated; keep the hypotheses separate.
A distributed low-rate scan is not a DDoS merely because many sources participate.
Server 5xx, timeout or latency alone is not attacker evidence; correlate cause and traffic behavior.
Normal popularity spikes may resemble floods; compare host, route, method, status, rate and historical baseline.
Evidence can support application-layer flood hypotheses without revealing request bodies or credentials.
Sentinel may alert on suspected availability abuse but remains OBSERVE_ONLY.
negative_knowledge: Do not call a scan DDoS from path breadth alone.
Do not call legitimate authenticated application navigation a scan from route breadth alone.
Do not infer attacker identity from subnet, ASN, geography or user-agent alone.
Do not convert a DDoS hypothesis into an autonomous firewall action.
learning_goal: Learn local normal load shape first, then distinguish discovery behavior from availability-pressure behavior with explicit supporting and conflicting evidence.
